#364. COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels

The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

The goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.

Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."

Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.

"For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.

"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.

Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."

Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.

"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance."

"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," said Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.

"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.

"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," said Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030."

But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."

David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, said the draft text showed a level of "seriousness" on important issues like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.

"The question is whether the level of ambition on those issues is carried through into the final outcome here," said Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days."

Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.

Update, November 17, 2026: This article has been updated with additional reactions to the draft text.

In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.

How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?

The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region's two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.

Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power.

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.

#361. The future of tech will not be inclusive by default

Ten years ago, QueerTech began with a feeling that too many 2SLGBTQI+ people in the technology sector know well: not belonging.

My co-founder Andy Saldaña and I were working at different companies in tech and kept running into the same frustration. We could see the possibility of the sector around us, had the skills to succeed, and believed technology, when stewarded responsibly, could change lives. Yet we could not see a place for ourselves, as queer professionals, within it.

I grew up in Morocco, where being queer was, and continues to be, illegal. In 2007, I left for New York City in pursuit of the "American Dream." There, I quickly realized this dream was based on a contradiction — opportunity without equal rights. Finally, I moved to Montreal, drawn to Canada’s reputation for respecting people across cultures, religions, and identities.

Across this journey, I expected geography to change my sense of belonging. It never did. So in 2016, Andy and I started small. QueerTech was a volunteer-run community group built around a simple need: to find one another, create connections, and make space for queer people in an industry where many of us felt invisible.

Today, QueerTech is a national nonprofit working across workforce development, entrepreneurship, research, responsible technology, and community. Our scale has changed, but the need has not. What has evolved is our understanding of what meaningful inclusion requires: not only creating spaces where queer people belong, but breaking down the systemic barriers that determine who gets access to opportunities, who advances into leadership, and who has the power to shape the future of technology.

The scope of our mission, spanning inclusive technology and professional wellbeing, demands ambitious goals and innovative programming grounded in collaboration and practical impact. Our community-first approach supports 2SLGBTQI+ professionals from industry entry through career advancement and entrepreneurship, while driving systemic change through partnerships with industry, investors, regulators, and community organizations.

QueerTech’s goals for the Canadian tech ecosystem are:

Increasing 2SLGBTQI+ representation to 20 percent across the sector.

Advancing 2SLGBTQI+ leadership representation to 5 percent.

Increasing funding for 2SLGBTQI+-owned ventures to 15 percent of total invested capital.

QT Access: Building pathways into tech through skills development, mentorship and career preparation.

QT Leaders: Advancing professionals into decision-making roles that shape workplace culture, policy and innovation.

QT Founders: Equipping queer entrepreneurs with tools, networks and access to capital.

QT Events: Creating safer spaces for connection, learning and opportunity, both in-person and online.

Our responsible technology priorities center on the QT Inclusive AI Initiative. Launched in 2026, it combines self-assessment tools, inclusive AI training, national research, community dialogue, practical governance frameworks and cross-sector partnerships to strengthen AI literacy, accountability, inclusive practices, and collaboration.

These efforts are grounded in a growing body of evidence about the barriers 2SLGBTQI+ professionals face, both within the technology sector and through the systems it creates. QueerTech’s 2026 research makes the scale of those challenges difficult to ignore.

QueerTech’s national Industry Census found 2SLGBTQI+ tech workers reported harassment and discrimination at roughly twice the rate of their non-2SLGBTQI+ peers: 44 percent reported harassment and 50 percent discrimination. Another 35 percent reported bias from AI hiring tools (versus 22 percent of peers). The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Inclusion in technology can no longer be measured only by who works inside the industry. We must also examine the systems the industry builds and deploys, including who participates in decisions, whose perspectives influence innovation, and who benefits from these advanced technologies.

This year, QueerTech studied both sides of that equation. Our research into AI development found 43 percent of Canadian technology companies reported limited to no formal processes for addressing bias, while 71 percent reported limited to no organizational support for equitable representation.

Our research into AI use in human resources also exposed a significant disconnect between institutional perceptions and queer professionals’ experiences. While 86 percent of HR professionals believed 2SLGBTQI+ employees were "comfortable being out," our 2026 Census found only 37 percent of queer professionals were "out" at work to a great extent — a disparity of nearly 50 percent.

The cost of that disconnect is higher than any one workplace. When queer professionals are overlooked, stalled or pushed out, companies lose skill, experience, and perspective. When people most likely to encounter bias are missing from product decisions, preventable blind spots can become features of automated systems and travel farther, faster and with less visibility.

That is not just an inclusion problem. It is a talent, product, and competitiveness problem for Canada’s innovation economy. As Canada invests in its technological future and digital sovereignty, we cannot afford to overlook talent, limit leadership access, or build technologies that fail to serve the people who depend on them.

The next question is what the sector does with that evidence.

On Nov. 18 and 19, more than 700 tech professionals will gather in Toronto for the 2026 QT Qonference (QTQ) under the theme Who Gets to Trust AI? This question is critical, given that trust in technology is shaped by various decentralized, and often competing, entities across the entire ecosystem. Developers build the systems. Employers decide how they are used. Executives set priorities. Policymakers create the rules. Workers and communities experience the results.

QTQ convenes these groups to address the same challenges from different perspectives. Better decisions happen when the people building, governing, and using technology are at the same table, but participation alone is not enough. Meaningful change requires institutions to translate conversation into action: removing barriers to opportunity, embedding accountability into technology development and deployment, and giving affected communities a meaningful role in shaping these technologies.

The future of tech will not be inclusive by default. It will be shaped by who is included in the decisions that define it. The responsibility belongs to all of us — industry leaders, investors, policymakers, and communities — to ensure that innovation expands opportunity rather than reinforces existing inequalities. Inclusion is not a concession to innovation; it’s a condition for responsible, sustainable innovation.

This article represents the opinion of its writer.

QueerTech is a national nonprofit advancing 2SLGBTQI+ talent, entrepreneurship, and inclusive technology across Canada’s tech ecosystem. Through community-led programming, original research, strategic partnerships, and actionable inclusion tools, QueerTech builds pathways to opportunity for queer professionals, leaders, and entrepreneurs while working with ecosystem partners to address the institutional barriers that limit access, advancement, and participation. Guided by its Vision 2034, QueerTech is working toward a technology ecosystem where queer people don't just participate — they thrive, lead, and help shape the future of innovation.

#360. Teenage swimmer breaks two world records in four days

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh said, per Reuters.

“It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.

#356. The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?

The Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has become a focal point for the far right. Many of its members and staff have ties to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations.

The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."

The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."

Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

This article was originally written in German.

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

“All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese said. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

“So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

“And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

In the same game, Clark said to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

“Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese said. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

LSU head coach Mulkey said she had “no clue” about what transpired.

#353. Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors

Malware cocktail delivers cryptocurrency theft payloads and iOS exploits, among other things.

Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.

ReportURI researcher Scott Helme said the delivery mechanism wasn’t a CDN cache poisoning attack, which uses HTTP to cause a CDN to cache harmful responses. Instead, the attack relied on Optimizely’s legitimate infrastructure, including its domains, to serve the tainted code. Optimizely’s own customer JavaScript for the www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com URLs were also affected.

“We don’t know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else,” ReportURI Helme wrote. “That’s for Optimizely to explain.”

Optimizely representatives didn’t respond to questions sent by email.

The scripts were named track.js, and all four components became active at the same time. Devices that received the malicious code responded differently depending on their platform and what they were doing on the final page delivering it. Actions performed included:

1. Crypto wallet address swapping. The script searches for wallet addresses for nine different cryptocurrencies and, when found, replaces them with one of the attacker’s. ReportURI said funds have already been stolen from some people whose devices ran the code.

2. Card skimming. The script watches HTTP requests for payment card numbers, expiry dates, and CVVs. When all three are present, it sends them to https://1688360.cc/card.php. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes such as Stripe and Adyen were unaffected.

4. The DarkSword and Coruna exploit kits for iOS. The kits are delivered through a file named boot.js served from 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and eil786npto9u5bq.icu. The file delivers a hidden iframe that contains an exploit chain tailored to the iOS version being used. Coruna can infect iOS versions 13 to 17. DarkSword can infect versions 18.x. A separate chain for iOS 26 fingerprints devices but doesn’t appear to do anything else. Earlier this month, researchers saw hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin attempting to deliver DarkSword through multiple vectors, including a compromised web analytics service.

The list of sites that ReportURI found delivering the malicious scripts numbers 178, and as noted, includes many big names. It’s unclear if the list is exhaustive. Helme said in an interview that “Ars wasn’t affected as far as we saw, and I haven’t seen any other indications it was.” Website administrators can check both the ReportURI post and this one from security firm Cynet for indicators of compromise.

At the moment, there’s no information available on how successful the exploit chains were in installing the payloads. Beyond the bare-bones details above, more precise information about what versions of iOS were susceptible was also unavailable. These sorts of gaps are common in breaking news concerning mass malware attacks, because it takes time for researchers to sift through the evidence. Readers are encouraged to check back as new developments come to light.

The indicators may help end users determine if they are affected, but the skill required is likely out of reach for many.

#351. AOC, Paris Hilton push for House vote on explicit deepfake bill

Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, socialite Paris Hilton, and others called for the House of Representatives to vote on the long-stalled, bipartisan DEFIANCE Act at a Capitol Hill press conference on Tuesday.

DEFIANCE stands for Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits, and the legislation would let survivors sue people who knowingly share, solicit, or receive sexually explicit and nonconsensual deepfakes (AI-generated images or video), according to a press release by anti-sexual violence organization RAINN.

The bill would also establish a 10-year statute of limitations that would begin when the survivor turns 18 or discovers the violation, whichever is later.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

The DEFIANCE Act passed the Senate unanimously on Jan. 13, 2026, after it had passed the first time in July 2024.

Since this Jan., the bill has stalled in the House.

Republican Rep. Laurel Lee of Florida, a cosponsor, said in a statement, "For too long, our laws have lagged behind this technology, leaving victims without clear legal tools when their likeness is stolen and weaponized. The DEFIANCE Act closes that gap."

At the press conference, Ocasio-Cortez stated, "Every single day that this bill does not pass, and every day that this bill is not signed into law, is a day that more children, women, and people are victimized with no recourse and that there is no accountability for abusers and predators."

"And so what it means is that thousands of people in this country, if not tens of thousands and eventually millions, could be subject to sexual abuse on our watch just due to complacency," Ocasio-Cortez continued.

Hilton, who has had hundreds of thousands of deepfakes created of her online, spoke up about the DEFIANCE Act in January, CBS News reported. She then joined yesterday's press conference along with Ocasio-Cortez, Lee, as well as survivors of tech-enabled sexual abuse and advocates Elliston Berry and Elizabeth Cline, and advocate and father Joseph Tucker Daniels, according to RAINN's press release.

Hilton said at the conference, "Ten months ago, I stood here at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent, and I asked Congress to do something about it."

"The laws aren't protecting us," Hilton continued. "And if this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might be feeling facing this completely alone."

If you have had intimate images shared without your consent, call the Cyber Civil Rights Initiative's 24/7 hotline at 844-878-2274 for free, confidential support. The CCRI website also includes helpful information as well as a list of international resources.

#349. Yet another satellite company is jockeying for a rocket—but this one makes sense

“Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most.”

Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company.

The announcement came as an all-cash voluntary tender offer from an Italian subsidiary of ICEYE to Avio’s shareholders, led by the Italian defense conglomerate Leonardo. Avio said its board of directors “has taken note of the notice” from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer.

Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. The Vega C has flown successfully seven times in eight attempts since 2022. It is a follow-on to an earlier version of the Vega rocket that amassed a 20-for-22 record since debuting in 2012.

ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, where access to private capital, regulatory barriers, and fragmented markets often hinder startup growth, according to a recent report from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ICEYE’s valuation stands at more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.

In a statement, ICEYE said it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements.

“Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most,” said Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and co-founder of ICEYE. “Avio has built the launch and propulsion capability Europe relies on. With ICEYE’s long-term capital behind it, we can integrate the supply chain, grow output and strengthen the European programs that already depend on it. Together we can build, launch and operate sovereign space systems end-to-end, made in Europe for governments across the world.”

Avio oversees the consortium of European companies that produces the Vega C rocket and conducts final assembly of Vega C rocket stages at its factory near Rome. For most of the Vega program’s history, Avio handed the rockets to French launch provider Arianespace, which managed marketing, sales, and launch day operations in French Guiana. Avio recently took over those responsibilities to bring the entire Vega C operation in-house.

ICEYE has built and launched 84 radar reconnaissance satellites, providing routine overhead imagery of locations around the world, even during darkness or cloud cover. In addition to its commercial satellite fleet, ICEYE has sold turnkey satellites directly to national governments, including Finland, Poland, Germany, Sweden, Portugal, Greece, and the Netherlands.

Last month, ICEYE announced a partnership with Nokia, another Finnish company, to develop a low-Earth orbit satellite constellation to support European connectivity needs, particularly in the defense and security sectors. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense announced a preliminary agreement, saying it intends to work with ICEYE and Nokia on the constellation, days after Ukraine reported new restrictions on its access to Starlink and Starshield broadband services offered by SpaceX.

“Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. “We must all rely on capabilities that we can control.”

There’s a long way to go before ICEYE and Nokia can start deploying their constellation, but their goal is to begin launching 50 satellites per year starting in 2028. The companies have not disclosed expected figures for throughput and latency on the network, or a total number of satellites for global or regional coverage. Depending on altitude, it would likely require hundreds or thousands of satellites. SpaceX has more than 11,000 operating satellites in its Starlink constellation today.

What is clear, however, is that ICEYE’s future radar and broadband satellites will need rides to space, and Avio’s Vega C rocket needs business. The primary customer for Vega C is the European Space Agency, and the rest of the rocket’s future schedule is largely filled with satellites from European national governments. Vega C’s purely commercial business line is thin.

Through the proposed transaction, ICEYE says it would secure more access to launch services, and Avio would receive investment for higher production and more frequent flights of the Vega rocket family, which averages fewer than three per year.

The most recent data indicates a dedicated Vega C launch sells for approximately $55 million, just shy of the commercial price for a much more powerful dedicated SpaceX Falcon 9. Nearly all of ICEYE’s satellites, except for the first-view demo spacecraft, have launched on Falcon 9 rideshare missions, which SpaceX intends to phase out after 2028. SpaceX sold rideshare launch slots for satellites of ICEYE’s size and mass for about $700,000. After accounting for potential savings after ICEYE’s potential purchase of Avio, an ICEYE satellite might be able to launch on Vega C for two to three times that price.

Avio and the European Space Agency are jointly funding the development of a new version of Vega, the Vega E, which replaces the top part of Vega C with a new higher-performing methane-fueled upper stage. ESA and Avio also signed a nearly $50 million contract last year to begin designing a reusable upper stage similar in concept and appearance to SpaceX’s Starship, although much smaller. The idea is to complete early design work on the reusable upper stage as a potential replacement for Vega E.

Business results seem to bear out the benefits of combining launch and satellite services under one roof. SpaceX’s Starlink network and Falcon 9 rocket would not have been as successful without the other. Rocket Lab, the No. 2 US launch company by launch rate, quickly branched out into satellite manufacturing after establishing the reliability of its Electron rocket. Pretty much every US launch provider has a role in satellite production or in-space services, or plans to, except for United Launch Alliance.

The coming launch crunch precipitated by SpaceX’s plans to retire the Falcon 9 has underscored the importance of assured access to space. SpaceX is prioritizing Starship launches for its own Starlink network and future Starmind AI satellites.

One of SpaceX’s competitors in the satellite broadband business, AST Space Mobile, announced last week that it is developing its own rocket to launch its communications network. It has launched most of its satellites to date on Falcon 9. Another company, Cowboy Space, plans to put orbiting data centers into space, bringing it into competition with SpaceX’s Starmind initiative. Cowboy Space, too, recently announced it was working on its own rocket.

There are reasons to disbelieve both companies’ launcher plans. Neither has any rocket development experience, and both are targeting first flights in 2028, a bewilderingly fast path to the launch pad. There are reasons to be skeptical of ICEYE and Avio, too, but if they do join forces, the combined company would boast established satellite and rocket production lines and backing from European governments seeking to reclaim sovereignty amid fraying ties with the United States.

#348. Alligators, pet snakes, a dog on a jet ski. Meet the animals of GTA 6.

Grand Theft Auto VI launches Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and as the game unlocks around the world, players are already sharing clips of their first encounters with the local wildlife.

Beyond the streets of Vice City, Leonida — Rockstar's fictional take on Florida — is home to more than 170 animal species according to Game Informer, from alligators (that can eat you!) and manatees to jellyfish and dogs of several breeds. That's a massive jump from the roughly 28 species in GTA 5. Here's what we know about the animals in GTA 6 so far, and what you can do when you find them.

The wildlife in Leonida gets pretty specific to Florida. There are the animals you'd probably expect, like flamingos, manatees, and alligators, plus a few that might surprise you, like green iguanas, cane toads, and rhesus macaques. Yes, Florida really does have monkeys. And if you head up to Mount Kalaga, it’s worth stopping to see what’s going on around you. One of Rockstar's screenshots shows a cougar stalking a group of deer, so mind your surroundings.

So far, people have spotted everything from armadillos, beavers, and raccoons to black bears, bobcats, and boars. There are also foxes, otters, skunks, squirrels, frogs, turtles, and snakes, plus cows, horses, cats, and dogs. And if you're the kind of person who stops to pet every dog you pass, there are already reports of Australian shepherds, Chihuahuas, Dobermans, German shepherds, Labradors, and Rottweilers.

There's plenty to look for along the water, too. Think pelicans, herons, and spoonbills, along with ducks, gulls, cormorants, cranes, and those flamingos. Eagles, pigeons, storks, and woodpeckers have also turned up. In the water itself, sightings range from crayfish, eels, and jellyfish to dolphins, sea turtles, manta rays, hammerhead sharks, and whales. If you go scuba diving off the Leonida Keys, some of the marine life even glows.

A few sightings are still up for debate. GTABase lists possums and rats, for example, while IGN left both off its list.

If you pass by an adorable cat or dog, you can pet both. Petting a cat actually gives Jason a small focus boost, and if a dog's owner gives you permission, you can give it a treat. Some gas stations sell pet treats, according to The Guardian, and you also have the option to praise or scold either animal.

You can also run into a cat while stealing a car. In one clip, Jason drives off, hears loud meowing, and suddenly has a cat lunging at him. A timed button prompt lets him fend it off, and from there, you can pull over and let the cat out or keep driving. As one user put it, "Cats Are Now Gangsters."

Apparently, dogs in Leonida like jet skis, too. One player in a post on X swam out to see how far they could get from shore and found a dog sitting on a jet ski that users can ride with. How it got out there is anybody's guess.

Back on dry land, Jason has a pet of his own. Dolores, a snake, lives at his house in the Leonida Keys, and feeding her a mouse gives him a small focus boost. So far, she's the only pet Jason can keep in the story, according to Cultured Vultures.

You can also keep track of the animals you see. Open the weapon wheel, select your binoculars, and zoom in on an animal. Then hold R1 on PlayStation or RB on Xbox to add it to your wildlife logbook. There are 62 types of birds to spot, as we covered in our GTA 6 birdwatching guide, and different breeds of cats and dogs get their own entries. Studying any 100 of the 255 entries counts toward 100 percent completion, according to PowerPyx.

There's also a zoo to visit, and you can go fishing or hunting. Rockstar North's Rob Nelson told YouTuber TGG that fishing is catch-and-release, so every fish goes back in the water, even during a challenge, as GameSpot reported.

Hunting is a way to earn money. Jason's old Army friend Bret Vogel teaches him how to track deer before sending him after other animals. Some hunting challenges spell out exactly what to look for. According to the outlet, some send players after a boar, a rattlesnake, and a panther.

One challenge, the Legendary Hunter challenge, asks players to hunt eight unique animals, whose identities are still under wraps. Perhaps one of which is this unrecognizable creature. #346. What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

#345. A Scattered Spider hacker just got 6 years in a U.S. prison

The spammers. The scammers. And you. Telemarketers and junk mail has evolved in the digital age to a behemoth of persistent trickery. In Scammed, we help you navigate a connected world that’s out for your money, your information, or just your attention.

Scattered Spider was once called "one of the most dangerous financial criminal groups" by Microsoft cybersecurity researchers. The U.S. has now closed the case against five of the group's members, sending the final defendant to prison for more than half a decade.

British Scattered Spider member Tyler Robert Buchanan has just been sentenced to six years in prison, according to the DOJ. Buchanan, who is 24 years old, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

The five Scattered Spider hackers took part in a massive phishing campaign which targeted employees of major technology companies, telecommunications companies, and entertainment companies between September 2021 and April 2023.

During this time, Scattered Spider carried out a massive phishing scheme where they posed as employers or their IT providers, spamming employees with text messages that urged them to log in to phishing websites. #344. San Diego dumps both Flock cameras and smart streetlights

500+ cameras will go dark just 3 years after mayor urged approval.

On Monday evening, San Diego’s city council voted to end its contracts with two surveillance equipment vendors, Flock and Ubicquia. San Diego is one of the largest cities to end its relationship with Flock, the startup with an estimated valuation of $8.3 billion.

“We fucking won!” said Lilly Irani of the Transparent and Responsible Use of Surveillance Technology (TRUST) SD Coalition, speaking in her personal capacity.

She and her colleagues have been among the loudest critics in recent years.

“The national energy creating left and right and center coalitions was the major cause [of the political victory],” she said, noting that it was only last month that one of the council members revoked his support, creating an opening for a political majority to halt the surveillance.

That council member, Stephen Whitburn, said in an October press conference that he wanted his fellow citizens to “feel safe.”

“If Flock cameras are causing many San Diegans to feel unsafe, then they have lost effectiveness as a public safety tool,” he said at the time.

After the Monday vote, San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said in a social media post that he “respect[ed] the Council’s decision” and would not veto the move to stop operation of the cameras across the city.

Andrew Smith, a spokesperson for Flock, told Ars in an email on Tuesday that the company also “respect[s] the city’s decision.” But Flock isn’t happy about it. “When a tool that is actively helping solve violent crimes is removed, public safety moves backward,” Smith wrote. “That has real consequences: cases will take longer to solve, organized retail theft crews will operate with fewer obstacles, a missing child may not be returned home, and victims may wait longer, or indefinitely, for justice.”

At Monday’s city council meeting, police representatives said there has been a 20 percent decline in vehicle theft since 2023, with 689 stolen vehicles recovered as a result of the Flock cameras.

The vote is a remarkable turnabout from just three years ago, when the mayor and other municipal leaders urged the city council to approve the program.

The city’s wholesale rejection of these devices included Ubicquia’s so-called “smart streetlights” that worked in concert with Flock’s AI-driven automatic license plate reader (ALPR) software. This cessation of smart streetlights marks the second time in less than a decade that San Diego has experimented with and then ultimately rejected this technology.

At one point, San Diego purchased thousands of smart streetlight systems from a different vendor, GE Current, but a previous mayoral administration shuttered them in 2020. After that, Ubicquia acquired the smart city platform and proposed a newer installation of 500 cameras in 2023 in partnership with Flock—and supported by police—which was installed in 2023.

“A reminder for every city, agency, and institution: if you create an advisory board of experts, listen to them!” she wrote. “Actually, earnestly listen to them. It’s cheaper than learning the hard way. Do better.”

That sentiment is echoed by Secure Justice, an Oakland-based advocacy group, which has been studying and monitoring Flock’s issues nationwide.

“We’ve documented at least 513 Flock contracts that have ended in red and blue states, in large and small cities,” Brian Hofer, the group’s executive director, emailed Ars. “It’s pretty clear that Americans do not consent to their government tracking them as we go about our daily lives.”

#343. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#341. Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it

Word, Excel, and PowerPoint now live inside Copilot; always-on agents are next.

Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them.

Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.

Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.

Copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment currently available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”

Trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s new frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he said.

In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft says each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.

The promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and users to place their trust in the company’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure must still be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will need to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.

Along with the guardrails, Microsoft announced what it calls the “AI Transparency Initiative.” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and MasterCard, to develop open, industry-wide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”

Along with the other announced additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365, its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The new agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft says is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”

Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics: “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” said Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model, and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less.”

Nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for users across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he said. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”

That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “community-first AI infrastructure plan.” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

#340. 5 old-school charging ports you probably forgot phones had before USB-C

Back when chargers were less standardized, we had some interesting connectors for phone power.

From its reversible design to improved power delivery and high-speed data transfers, USB-C is the connector to beat for smartphones today. A sweeping EU mandate cemented its pole position in the race toward a universal standard. Earlier ports, charming as they were, were often bulkier and not as feature-rich. The lack of a universal connector led to a significant amount of e-waste from switching chargers every time you tried a phone from a new manufacturer.

Despite their limited bandwidth and slower charging speeds, I can't help but look back fondly at these unique connectors from the old days. They came in all shapes and sizes based on what manufacturers thought their customers wanted and what was technically feasible at the time. Before features like Apple's AirDrop, you had to rely on a physical cable to transfer large files, and your collection might have been huge if you jumped between phone manufacturers.

Let's check out some of the old-school, sometimes forgotten or even bizarre, charging ports that made it into yesteryear's phones before the advent of USB-C.

First seen on Motorola phones in 2000, the 17-pin CE Bus connector was gigantic. While it wasn't reversible and had hooks that kept it in place, the connector was notable for managing power, data and audio together. It was used in the Motorola V60, one of the most recognizable models of the clamshell era. The first phone with iTunes support, the Motorola ROKR E1, also launched with the port.

Thinner phones like the Razr V3 switched over to Mini-USB, making the CE Bus connector obsolete. Other companies moving toward Mini-USB also helped lower costs, compared to having tons of proprietary solutions to transfer data or charge devices.

Nokia's Pop-Port connector was built with external accessories in mind, from earphones to data transfer cables. Owners of the famed Nokia 7210 from 2002 will remember its 14-pin port supporting camera accessory add-ons and car kits. It wasn't very secure, however, and its plastic clips wore down with time. This made listening to music a chore, especially when you went jogging.

While the Pop-Port could be used for charging, Nokia devices of the time usually relied on a separate 2.0 mm thin-tip barrel connector instead. As Mini-USB ports became common, the Pop-Port slowly faded from existence.

Apple's proprietary power connector first showed up in 2003 on the third-gen iPod. This flat and wide port was then used across the first iPhone and iPad models. Speaker systems like Bose's SoundDock and Apple's iPod Hi-Fi also relied on the port. All those pins in the connector helped ensure support for FireWire, Apple's legacy charging standard, in its early appearances.

Apple replaced it with the reversible and smaller 8-pin Lightning connector in 2012, another proprietary option that kept the Apple camp from using chargers compatible with Android devices. These connectors also housed small chips to regulate voltage, which let the company collect licensing fees when third-party manufacturers used it for accessories. In 2018, the iPad Pro made the switch to USB-C and the iPhone 15 lineup followed suit in 2023.

Built to handle data transfers, charging and audio output, the clunky FastPort showed up in 2005 on the Sony Ericsson K750i. With double-sided plastic hooks that snapped onto matching holes on the device, the flimsy 12-pin connection was reminiscent of a VGI port's screws. If a hook were to break, the plug would no longer snap into place, creating a huge pain.

Despite its flaws, the FastPort's versatility pointed in the direction the mobile industry would take as it hunted for a universal standard. It was replaced by the Micro-USB and 3.5 mm audio jack combo in 2010. A five-year run might not be much in tech time, but its unconventional shape remains iconic to this day.

The HTC Dream, the first commercially available Android phone, featured the chunky 11-pin ExtUSB port, also known as Extended USB. Recognizable by its slanted corner, it combined the 5-pin Mini-USB port with extra pins that granted it data, power and audio capabilities. Fortunately, that meant regular Mini-USB chargers were compatible with this legacy port.

The connector was exclusive to HTC's early Android devices and Windows Mobile phones before they switched to Micro-USB ports. For a time, phones with this port dropped the 3.5 mm headphone jack long before Apple removed it from the iPhone, forcing users to purchase ExtUSB adapters to connect their headphones.

#339. How long it takes to play GTA 6: Story playthrough and achievements

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here. The launch day for the highly anticipated video game has arrived, more than 13 years after its predecessor.

If you patiently waited more than a decade for GTA 6, you're probably hoping for a long, immersive experience that makes it worth the wait.

Good news! Reports are now coming in from game reviewers, and it seems like you're in for a treat. You'll likely be playing GTA 6 for a long time.

An early report from Insider Gaming suggested GTA 6 will take around 50 hours to complete the main campaign. Now that the wider review embargo has lifted, we can get an even more nuanced idea of how long it will take to finish the 91 main story missions GTA 6 has to offer.

For example, our friends at IGN polled four different players who had finished the game, and each of them had something different to say. One player finished the story in "just" 42 hours, which was the lowest estimate. Another took 65 hours, and then a third took 72 hours. Finally, IGN reviewer Luke Reilly said he needed a whopping 115 hours to complete the game.

To be clear, those figures represent the amount of time it took each writer to complete GTA 6's main campaign. If you want to fully complete everything in the game, you're looking at a much longer gameplay time. Much longer.

Aside from GTA 6's main campaign, there are also side quests and an array of interactions, events, and locations to explore. Gamers will likely want to unlock the reported 55 achievements, including the Platinum Trophy and the Mythic achievement.

If you want to do all of that, you could be looking at potentially at least 200 hours of gameplay for GTA 6.

That's not even counting any time spent just wandering the streets of Vice City or cruising around in a car while listening to the stacked GTA 6 soundtrack and radio stations.

So, lock in, gamers (and please take plenty of breaks). More than 200 hours of GTA 6 await.
